newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Gunfire in Kisangani as first Zaire aid arrives.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire in Kisangani as first Zaire aid arrives.

text.p: Sporadic gunshots rang out in Kisangani as flights paving the way for humanitarian assistance arrived in the eastern Zaire city.

The burial on Wednesday of a soldier of the feared civil guard, killed as he was trying to prevent overnight looting, prompted bursts of automatic fire into the air at his graveside from angry comrades.
People avoided the main streets of the riverside city of 500,000 and many traders left the central market, fearing that occasional shots could turn into looting.

Kisangani is the only feasible bridgehead inside Zaire for humanitarian operations across a massive area of forests and hills where tens of thousands of displaced Zaireans, along with Rwandan and Burundian refugees may be in hiding.
Fighting between Zaire's army and Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsi rebels has spread chaos through the east of the vast Central African state.
The United States and Britain said on Wednesday they were prepared to join a U.N. military operation to save the civilians, ending days of uncertainty over the mission.
Church officials on Wednesday said flights arrived with aid from Belgium and equipment for the International Committee of the Red Cross.
"Now we're getting some assistance we have to work out a plan to be able to get it down to the places where it is needed," said Brother Gerard Selenke of the Roman Catholic church.
There were no reports of shooting at the airport, 17 km (10 miles) from the city centre.

Efforts to get aid down to areas where the displaced are thought to be concentrated have been hampered by the insecurity brought about by the retreat of soldiers from battle fronts around Bukavu and Goma.
"The area will soon be stable, as those who arrive here are now being moved back to their positions," said regional governor Lombeya Bosongo.
Local forces try to prevent the new arrivals from looting businesses and homes.

Aid workers with trucks sent by the church and the local business association have reached Lubutu, 200 km (125 miles) away with medicines. They report many displaced people, but even the estimates are vague and vary between thousands and tens of thousands.
No vehicle has yet reached Walikale 350 km (220 miles) from Kisangani, where even more displaced and refugees are believed to have stopped.
Displaced Zaireans continue to arrive in Kisangani, having been able to make part of the journey along the single bad road by car or truck, and completing the rest by foot.
Claude Olenga, administrator of the Catholic charity CARITAS on Tuesday told Reuters as many as 1,000 could now be in the city.
